items.title: Researchers introduce Kimi Linear, a hybrid linear attention architecture that outperforms full attention across short and long contexts and reinforcement learning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Kimi Linear: An Expressive, Efficient Attention Architecture (2025)
items.summary:
Kimi Linear is a new attention architecture featuring Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), which extends Gated DeltaNet with a finer-grained gating mechanism to better utilize finite-state RNN memory. The design includes a chunkwise algorithm using specialized Diagonal-Plus-Low-Rank transition matrices to improve hardware efficiency and reduce computation compared to general DPLR formulations.

The team pretrained a 3-billion activated parameter model combining KDA and Multi-Head Latent Attention, demonstrating superior performance over full MLA across various tasks while reducing key-value cache usage by up to 75% and increasing decoding throughput up to six times for a 1 million token context. The researchers have open-sourced the KDA kernel, vLLM implementations, and released pretrained and instruction-tuned model checkpoints to support further research.

items.originalTitle: The Actual Reason Why Google "Fell Out" of the AI Race Changes Everything
items.summary:
Google's apparent retreat from the AI race is attributed to a strategic decision led by DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis, who favors developing world models that simulate real-world understanding rather than pursuing recursive self-improvement methods championed by startups like OpenAI and Anthropic. This shift reflects a fundamental divergence in AI research philosophy and places Google in a high-stakes position to either lead or fall behind in future AI advancements.

While OpenAI and Anthropic rapidly advance AI through autonomous coding agents and large-scale compute, Google is investing in alternative approaches that may take longer but aim for more comprehensive artificial general intelligence. Despite public appearances of competition, insiders suggest Google has effectively withdrawn from the current AI race to focus on this different path, leveraging its existing business to sustain long-term AI research efforts.

This strategic divergence highlights a broader contest between startup-driven rapid innovation and incumbent-backed foundational research, with significant implications for the future direction of AI development and industry leadership.

items.title: Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: A Technical Timeline of the July 2026 Incident [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: A Technical Timeline of the July 2026 Incident
items.summary:
Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: A Technical Timeline of the July 2026 Incident

Hugging Face just released this extremely detailed technical description of OpenAI's recent accidental cyberattack against their infrastructure. This attack was very sophisticated, and the resulting document doubles as a crash-course in modern adversarial security approaches.

We're still waiting for more details from OpenAI on how their agent broke out of its sandbox. The package proxy that it found a zero-day vulnerability in has now been confirmed as JFrog's Artifactor, and JFrog and OpenAI Collaboration on Zero-Day Security Findings from JFrog links to the Artifactory 7.161.15 release notes which list 8 separate CVEs credited to OpenAI staff members.

Having broken out through the HTTP proxy, the agent started by establishing a base of operations for the rest of the attack:

[...] the agent escaped its sandbox by exploiting a zero-day in the package registry cache proxy, one of its primary permitted network egress with internet, then abused a public code-evaluation external sandbox hosted on a third-party provider's infrastructure. It was able to run commands as root/admin on that external sandbox and used it as a control, staging, and egress base for the entire campaign: it acted as an external launchpad for the agent.

(That "third-party provider" turned out to be Modal.)

It then spent five days - from Thursday 8th to Monday 13th July - executing a classic attack pattern: establishing C2 (command and control), reconnaissance, escalating privileges, dumping configuration information, exfiltrating the target data, and cleaning up after itself.

(The first Hugging Face post about the incident followed on Thursday 16th, and OpenAI's confession came on Tuesday 21st.)

Along the way it used all kinds of neat tricks. At one point it found an unsafe Jinja2 template execution and used it to execute arbitrary code:

{{ cycler.__init__.__globals__.__builtins__.exec( "import gzip,base64; exec(gzip.decompress(base64.b64decode('<payload>')))" ) }}

It broke out of a container within Hugging Face, stole a Kubernetes service-account token, and used that to further explore the network.

It monkey-patched the Python socket library to hard-code an IP address when "DNS got in the way":

socket.getaddrinfo = lambda *a, **k: [(2, 1, 6, '', ('<pinned-ip>', 443))]

It even fired up its own Tailscale network to help exfiltrate data!

tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking \ --state=mem: --socket=/tmp/ts.sock \ --socks5-server=127.0.0.1:1055 \ --no-logs-no-support >/tmp/td 2>&1 &

The Hugging Face team note that, while a human attacker could have discovered and used the same exploits, the key difference here was speed:

Our learning from this type of attack is that machine-speed offense makes ordinary weaknesses more expensive for defenders. LLM agents bring a step increase in the number of paths an attacker can test, the speed at which failed paths can be replaced, and the volume of evidence defenders must interpret.

What's clear to me from this is that the very best frontier models, unencumbered by additional guardrails, will find an exploit if there is one to be found.

The entire software industry needs to up its security game.

items.originalTitle: Cursor Customers Fight Price Hikes in Contract Talks
items.summary:
Cursor, the pioneering AI coding app, is growing pretty well ahead of SpaceX’s planned $60 billion purchase. But the company, which provides access to different AI models for coding work, last year shifted to charging more customers based on usage rather than flat rate subscriptions, and the move is now causing some heated contract renewal discussions. That seems to be pushing some customers to shift to Claude Code and other AI coding apps.

items.originalTitle: OpenAI and Anthropic Are Quietly Teaming Up in Washington
items.summary:
OpenAI and Anthropic are arch enemies whose leaders can’t stand each other. But the two foes have formed an unholy alliance in Washington in the interest of self-preservation. 

With the Trump administration set to finalize its framework for regulating and evaluating “frontier models” by August 1, the two leading AI developers are quietly lobbying D.C. on a shared agenda: making sure lagging competitors like Meta and SpaceXAI also have to comply with government reviews of their models, and raising alarms about Chinese open-source models.

Their alignment isn’t obvious at first glance. But our sources tell us Anthropic and OpenAI have pushed to expand the type of models that would require government review under the framework to include those from their competitors. (They’ve discussed how the government and industry can develop an evaluation to determine whether a model requires extended review, based on its capabilities in cybersecurity or other tasks that could present national security risks.)

Some of those rivals have disagreed, preferring that the government focus on Anthropic and OpenAI’s models, given that those models are considered to be the most capable (and thus potentially dangerous and in need of a review).

items.summary:
Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI, flush from the breakout success of its recently released model, Kimi K3, is already discussing plans for Kimi K4, which would be significantly larger in size than K3, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. There’s just one problem: To train that new model, Moonshot would need access to more of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips, which U.S. rules dictate should not be available to Chinese firms.

Despite those restrictions, Moonshot trained Kimi K3—the world’s largest open-source model, with 2.8 trillion parameters—on Nvidia chips, including the most advanced Blackwell ones, according to three people with knowledge of the matter, confirming part of a statement in an X post by White House senior official Michael Kratsios. Moonshot is now seeking access to more Blackwell chips to prepare for the development of future-generation models such as K4, according to two of the people.

importance.development_summary: The New York Times is engaged in a high-profile legal battle against OpenAI and Microsoft over alleged copyright infringement related to AI training data. The case highlights broader challenges to press freedom, including government subpoenas targeting journalists and the impact of AI on journalism practices. The Times is cautious about AI adoption in journalism, emphasizing human oversight and the risks of premature reliance on AI-generated content.
